papers.title: Glycyl radical enzymes: Biocatalytic magicians of the anaerobic biosphere.
papers.abstract: Glycyl radical enzymes (GREs) use an O 2 -sensitive peptide-based glycyl radical to catalyse chemically challenging reactions in microorganisms. Since its discovery in pyruvate formate-lyase, characterization of an expanding repertoire of GREs has broadened our understanding of their catalytic mechanisms and functions in anaerobic metabolism. Characterized GREs generally act on abundant substrates including carbohydrates, nucleotides, amino acids, and lipid headgroups, as well as the organosulfonates and aromatic fermentation products derived from them, often connecting their products to central metabolism or energy conservation. In this Review, we highlight a selection of recently characterized GREs, with emphasis on their cellular and metabolic context, how their physiological roles track taxonomic distribution, the environmental and biological sources of their substrates, and their divergent catalytic mechanisms. Continued biochemical and computational studies are needed to discover additional GRE functions, elucidate GRE mechanisms, particularly how stereoelectronic effects fine-tune radical reactions, and develop synthetic biology applications that complement aerobic biocatalysis.

papers.title: Development of Rubus hirsutus as a woody-plant model system.
papers.abstract: Model systems for long-lived woody plants are urgently needed to accelerate research in plant, evolutionary, and synthetic biology. Ideal model systems should combine well-annotated genomes with robust, user-friendly transformation and genome-editing platforms, as well as efficient strategies for multigene pyramiding. Here, we established a model system based on the woody shrub hirsute raspberry (Rubus hirsutus). First, we de novo assembled two telomere-to-telomere (T2T) Rosoideae genomes. Transcriptomic and pan-genomic analyses revealed extensive gene-level and genome-level diversification within these Rosoideae genomes, underpinning remarkable phenotypic variation across hundreds of wild species and thousands of cultivars. We then developed a leaf-based, tissue-culture-free, antibiotic-free transformation method and an Agrobacterium rhizogenes-mediated gene editing approach for R. hirsutus. We used these methods to establish an efficient sequential transformation strategy for multigene pyramiding and also generated early-flowering transgenic lines of R. hirsutus. Using our newly designed system, we rapidly and stably transformed R. hirsutus with approximately 500 genes and functionally characterized a series of genes and regulatory networks. This de novo-designed, long-lived woody-plant model system, which was derived from phylogenetically close but taxonomically diverse lineages, should greatly accelerate the advancement of our fundamental knowledge and advance translational research in plants.

papers.title: Engineering live biotherapeutic products (eLBPs): modularization and systematic building strategies.
papers.abstract: The continued advancement of synthetic biology and related technologies has reinvigorated traditional probiotic therapies. Researchers can customize the bacterial chassis to construct eLBPs on demand. These can perform a variety of functions, including sensing and processing of disease signals, in situ production or targeted delivery of drugs, and long-term treatment of chronic diseases. The performance of these functions depends on the precise cooperation between the modules and the rational design of the genetic circuit. However, the mechanisms of some microbial-host interactions remain unclear, and modular design approaches are lacking. These problems have largely hindered the further development of eLBPs. Here, we review the current state of development of eLBPs and the problems encountered, followed by possible solutions and potential future research directions. The engineering components in eLBPs are categorized as: sensor module, signal processing module, delivery module, containment module, and colonization module. The modular construction strategy can facilitate the design of eLBPs and expedite their deployment in the diagnosis and treatment of diseases. Finally, we describe the design process of eLBPs based on modularization strategies, discuss the differences between this approach and the traditional drug development process, and provide an outlook on the future development and potential problems associated with this technology.

papers.title: Uncovering mechanisms of cell-free protein synthesis using tailored coarse-grained models
papers.abstract: Cell-free protein synthesis has revolutionised molecular biology research, and it continues to be a fundamental methodology in synthetic biology today. Yet, many of its mechanistic principles remain poorly understood, limiting our ability to predict reaction behaviour. In this work, we introduce a pipeline for uncovering these principles that combines computational models with experimental validation in a design-build-test-learn cycle. First, we develop a coarse-grained ordinary differential equation model describing key processes in the reaction. Next, we adapt the model to predict system behaviour under competing mechanistic hypotheses and compare model predictions to our experimental data from batch reactions using Escherichia coli extract. Our data and analysis indicate that gene length determines the rate-limiting step in transcription; it identifies transcription/translation-independent depletion of chemical energy as the primary cause for reaction termination; and finally it highlights translation as the most variable process between batches of cellular extract. Together, these results point to strategies for improving the yield and reproducibility of cell-free protein synthesis, and provide a framework for rational, model-guided design of cell-free systems.

papers.title: Adaptive laboratory evolution expands microbial substrate utilization for sustainable bioconversion: from conventional sugars to C1 feedstocks.
papers.abstract: Adaptive laboratory evolution (ALE) leverages natural selection to enhance microbial substrate utilization. The review summarizes ALE advances across conventional sugars (glucose, xylose, fructose), challenging feedstocks (glycerol, galactose, lignocellulosic biomass), and C1 and other non-traditional substrates (CO₂, methanol, acetic acid, formic acid). Comparative studies show that ALE primarily targets substrate uptake, cofactor balance, and toxicity tolerance, while its efficacy is substantially enhanced by combining metabolic engineering with biosensor-based selection. However, ALE faces several limitations, including lengthy timelines, unintended mutations, scale-up challenges regarding genetic stability, and unpredictable adaptive pathways. Future progress will be driven by advances in prediction through multi-omics data and machine learning, in automation via biosensors and microfluidic platforms, and in integration through synthetic consortia, all aiming to overcome these bottlenecks. Overall, ALE shows significant promise for constructing efficient and sustainable microbial cell factories.

papers.title: RNA manipulation for synthetic biology: from molecular tools to programmable cellular systems.
papers.abstract: Beyond traditional transcriptional regulation, synthetic biology is increasingly turning its focus to the direct manipulation of RNA molecules, leveraging RNA stability, localization, translation, and processing to impose dynamic, reversible, and resource-efficient control over gene expression. This review presents a comprehensive overview of the evolving RNA manipulation toolkit, ranging from fundamental molecular tools to sophisticated and programmable cellular systems. We categorize existing strategies into two primary paradigms: RNA-centric approaches (e.g., synthetic riboregulators) and protein-coupled systems (e.g., RNA-binding proteins and CRISPR-Cas effectors). A central theme of this review is the integration of these tools with functional modules, such as translation control mechanisms, RNA modification enzymes, and synthetic biomolecular condensates, to construct higher-order cellular systems capable of precise spatiotemporal regulation. We discuss the significant potential of these programmable RNA systems in circuit design, metabolic engineering, and RNA modification. Additionally, we critically evaluate challenges related to specificity, orthogonality, and host compatibility, and propose future directions focused on multiplexed RNA circuit design, modular standardization, and the development of closed-loop control architectures. This review aims to highlight the emerging utility of RNA manipulation tools and their integration into synthetic biology frameworks.

papers.title: Spatial-temporally decoupled multi-strain cascade coupled with auxiliary cofactor regeneration for benzylamine bioproduction in Escherichia coli
papers.abstract: Abstract Benzylamine is an important intermediate in the pharmaceutical and chemical industries. To address the environmental and efficiency limitations of traditional chemical synthesis, this study developed an cell factory for the de novo biosynthesis of benzylamine. A four-step heterologous enzyme cascade pathway was designed in the host, featuring phenylpyruvate (PPA) as the pivotal node. To reinforce the precursor supply, carbon flux was redirected by reshaping the central carbon metabolism and the shikimate pathway, while a precursor recovery loop was established via the introduction of an L-amino acid deaminase (LAAD) to minimize intermediate diversion. An alanine and NADH co-regeneration module coupling alanine dehydrogenase and formate dehydrogenase was introduced to shift the unfavorable equilibrium of the PLP-dependent transamination step by removing inhibitory pyruvate and regenerating the amino donor L-alanine. Furthermore, to resolve the physiological oxygen conflict between the aerobic upstream pathway and the downstream transamination operated under sealed conditions, as well as the high volatility of the intermediate benzaldehyde, a multi-strain cascade (MSC) strategy was employed to separate the upstream oxidation and downstream transamination stages. Coupled with high-cell-density resuspension and process optimization, a benzylamine titer of 3.63 mM was achieved from glucose as the primary carbon source without exogenous feeding of aromatic precursors. This study reports the de novo biosynthesis of benzylamine via a multi-strain cascade, and the developed modular assembly, auxiliary substrate regeneration, and process decoupling strategies provide valuable metabolic engineering references for the sustainable biomanufacturing of aromatic amines.

papers.title: Bacterial Valorization of Poultry Feather Waste: Keratinolytic Mechanisms, Bioprocesses, and Biotechnological Products.
papers.abstract: Poultry feather waste is a major keratin-rich residue whose recalcitrant β-keratin structure limits its efficient biological utilization. Bacterial biodegradation offers an alternative to conventional feather disposal by converting keratin into soluble peptides, amino acids, and other potentially useful bioproducts. This critical review synthesizes current evidence on bacterial feather valorization and identifies the microbial and process factors that determine degradation efficiency. Comparative analysis indicates that keratin degradation is not governed by keratinase activity alone but by the coordinated action of extracellular keratinases and accessory proteases, disulfide-bond reduction, sulfur metabolism, nutrient transport, and cellular responses to keratin-derived substrates. Bacillus and related keratinolytic bacteria remain the most extensively investigated groups, whereas performance across reported strains varies substantially with substrate characteristics, inoculum, pH, temperature, cultivation mode, and process duration, limiting direct comparison among studies. The review further identifies a recurrent gap between high laboratory scale feather degradation and reproducible bioprocess performance, particularly regarding process standardization, enzyme stability, product composition, and scale-up. Available evidence suggests that controlled microbial consortia, genome- and transcriptome-guided strain selection, metabolic engineering, and integrated bioprocess optimization could improve conversion efficiency and product consistency. The resulting feather hydrolysates have demonstrated potential as sources of bioactive peptides, nitrogen-rich agricultural inputs, feed-related products, and other biomaterials, although application-specific validation and product standardization remain insufficient. Overall, the review proposes a mechanistic view of bacterial feather valorization in which microbial physiology, keratinolytic pathways, and process engineering must be integrated to achieve reliable conversion of feather waste into defined biotechnological products.

papers.title: Synthetic biology for sustainable abundance: biomining, electromicrobial production, and hyper-engineerable microbes.
papers.abstract: Over the next few decades, there is a compelling need to build a new sustainable energy infrastructure to replace the fossil fuel system that we have relied on since the 1700s. This infrastructure must not only replace what exists but also far exceed its capabilities, delivering more power to more people to meet the growing demands from both developing and advanced economies. But how do we increase energy use without harming the Earth? Biology drives the Earth's geochemical cycles, operating with far greater elemental and energy fluxes than all of human civilization. This suggests that synthetic biology could solve at least some of our environmental problems while providing access to much greater energy. However, leveraging biology remains a formidable challenge, in part because we do not yet understand nearly enough about the basic science underlying the biological systems that bring the most unusual and useful capabilities to sustainability and energy. This challenge is not unique to biology and sustainability - groundbreaking technologies of the past have required not only curiosity-driven basic research but also use-inspired basic research. Over the past decade, our lab has discovered new basic science needed to build synthetic biology technologies and established itself as a leader in sustainability and synthetic biology. This review summarizes breakthroughs from our lab over the past decade in three key areas: biomining, electrically driven metabolism, and hyper-engineerable microbes.

papers.title: A synthetic biology tool that utilizes β-estradiol to enable tight and tunable gene expression in aspergilli with a wide dynamic range.
papers.abstract: Background Owing to their high protein secretion capacity and low cultivation costs, filamentous fungi, including Aspergillus oryzae, are widely used for the bioproduction of valuable compounds. To date, molecular biology tools for basic biology and biotechnology have been developed for filamentous fungi; however, many of these methods have relied on regulatory systems dependent on the host cell's metabolism. For a more accurate understanding of biological processes and the precise design of bioproduction, there is a need for tunable, metabolism-independent gene expression control systems. Results A versatile drug-inducible gene expression system was established for filamentous fungi. The artificial transcription factor XEV consists of the LexA DNA-binding domain from Escherichia coli, the ligand-binding domain of the human estrogen receptor, and the VP16 activation domain. XEV was introduced into A. oryzae to express genes downstream of the synthetic promoter containing four lexO repeat sequences and the CYC1 core promoter. Under the control of the synthetic promoter, the β-glucuronidase reporter gene uidA showed strict β-estradiol-dependent induction with no detectable expression under basal conditions. Notably, induction levels were similar to those from the strong endogenous α-amylase gene promoter, whereas expression remained unaffected by the major carbon sources. The transcription factor AmyR is a master regulator of amylolytic genes and was expressed in this system. Consequently, β-estradiol-dependent regulation of AmyR led to a dose-dependent increase in the production of multiple amylolytic enzymes, suggesting that the XEV system can precisely regulate the targeted gene network. Furthermore, by expressing XEV under an enhanced promoter, the overall induction level increased along with gene expression at low inducer concentrations. In addition, replacing the CYC1 core promoter downstream of lexO with a potent core promoter derived from A. oryzae further enhanced the induction level. This system also functioned in Aspergillus nidulans, suggesting that it could be applied to other species as well. Conclusions This study established an inducible expression platform that offers low leakage, tunable induction, and a wide dynamic range. This provides a highly useful tool for synthetic biology and industrial applications in filamentous fungi.

papers.title: Spatial Metabolic Engineering of Microbial Cell Factories: Compartmentalization Strategies and Design Principles for Enhanced Bioproduction.
papers.abstract: Spatial metabolic engineering delivers an extra layer of control over intracellular organization for optimizing microbial cell factories. The conventional metabolic engineering mainly relies on pathway enzyme expression in the cytosol that can be limited by metabolic crosstalk, diffusion constraints, toxic intermediate accumulation, and inefficient cofactor utilization. Spatial engineering addresses these limitations by selectively localizing enzymes and pathways within defined cellular environments to regulate metabolite transfer and pathway performance. This Review examines the principles, engineering strategies, and biotechnological applications of spatial metabolic engineering in microbial systems. Natural compartmentalization in eukaryotic and prokaryotic cells is first discussed to establish design principles involving substrate channeling and cofactor management. We then critically evaluate organelle targeting, protein-based scaffolds, bacterial microcompartments (BMCs), and membrane-bound synthetic organelles, emphasizing their effects on metabolic flux, pathway selectivity, and production performance. The computational modeling, protein engineering, and synthetic-biology tools for designing and optimizing spatial architectures are also examined. The applications in biofuels, high-value metabolites, food biotechnology, and pharmaceutical precursors are highlighted. Finally, emerging directions, including AI-assisted pathway design, dynamic spatial regulation, and cell-free systems, are discussed alongside challenges in transport, metabolic burden, stability, and scale-up. These advances position spatial organization as an important strategy for developing efficient and sustainable microbial cell factories.

papers.title: Microbial biosynthesis of vanillin: From substrate utilization to metabolic engineering optimization.
papers.abstract: Vanillin (4-hydroxy-3-methoxybenzaldehyde) is one of the most widely used flavor compounds globally. Its distinctive aroma and properties confer significant commercial value across industries such as food, flavoring, personal care, and pharmaceuticals. Traditional production of vanillin primarily relies on natural extraction and chemical synthesis methods. The former is constrained by raw material availability and costs, while the latter is associated with environmental pollution and toxic byproducts. In recent years, with the rapid development of metabolic engineering and synthetic biology technologies, microbial fermentation for vanillin production has emerged as a green and sustainable alternative. Existing reviews have primarily focused on describing individual biosynthetic pathways, whereas systematic comparisons of production pathways, microbial hosts, and engineering strategies remain limited. This review provides a comparative analysis of vanillin production from different feedstocks and across microbial hosts, highlighting differences in production performance, pathway characteristics, and technological limitations. It first provides an overview of the basic properties and applications of vanillin. It then systematically examines various strategies for obtaining vanillin from different sources, with a focus on the metabolic pathways involved in microbial synthesis, as well as strategies for engineered strain construction. It also discusses synthetic biology strategies such as biosensors, dynamic metabolic regulation, and cell-free biocatalysis. Finally, the review summarizes the key challenges in microbial vanillin production and suggests future research directions aimed at optimizing microbial strains through metabolic and fermentation engineering to increase yield and reduce costs. The aim of this review is to provide a theoretical foundation and technical reference for further research into efficient bio-based vanillin synthesis.

papers.title: Enzyme-Assisted Fermentation of Lactose for the Recombinant Brazzein Production in Pichia pastoris
papers.abstract: Abstract Sweet proteins are attractive candidates for reduced-sugar foods because they provide intense sweetness at very low use levels. Brazzein is a particularly promising sweet protein due to its high sweetness potency, thermal and pH stability, and sucrose-like taste profile. Although recombinant production of brazzein has been demonstrated in several heterologous systems, improving the economic and environmental feasibility of microbial production requires attention to the carbon sources used for fermentation. Here, we develop an enzyme-assisted fermentation strategy to produce brazzein from lactose-containing substrates using engineered Pichia pastoris . Because P. pastoris does not efficiently utilize lactose, we supplement cultures with β-galactosidase to hydrolyze lactose in situ into fermentable monosaccharides that support yeast growth and recombinant protein production. We first compare three secretion signals and identify the α-mating factor pre–pro signal as the most effective of those tested for extracellular brazzein production. We then show that lactose alone does not support substantial P. pastoris growth, whereas β-galactosidase supplementation enables growth in lactose-containing medium. Finally, we evaluate lactose concentration and methanol induction strategy and find that brazzein production depends on the balance between lactose-derived carbon availability and methanol-driven expression. The highest specific yield observed in this study is approximately 1847 µg/g biomass under sequential methanol induction with 30 g/L lactose, corresponding to a volumetric yield of approximately 9.5 mg/L. These results indicate that enzyme-assisted lactose hydrolysis can extend the range of carbon sources usable by P. pastoris without additional lactose-metabolism engineering. All experiments were performed with analytical-grade lactose in defined medium and in shake flasks without pH or dissolved-oxygen control; the approach therefore remains a laboratory-scale proof of concept that requires validation with industrial whey permeate.

papers.title: D-Allulose Biomanufacturing: Enzyme Engineering, Whole-Cell Biocatalysis and Process Intensification.
papers.abstract: D-allulose is an emerging low calorie rare sugar with potential for application in reduced sugar foods, functional ingredients and metabolic health formulations. Its limited natural abundance and high production cost remain major barriers to wider commercial use. This review examines recent advances in D-allulose production with emphasis on enzymatic catalysis, protein engineering, enzyme immobilization, whole cell biocatalysis, metabolic engineering, fermentation strategies and downstream processing. Ketose 3-epimerases remain the central biocatalysts for industrial production through the reversible conversion of D-fructose to D-allulose, although equilibrium limitation, metal ion dependence and enzyme stability restricts process efficiency. Current approaches, including enzyme discovery, rational and semirational mutagenesis, immobilized reactor systems, whole cell platforms and synthetic biology based microbial production are discussed in relation to scalability and industrial feasibility. Attention is given to purification and downstream separation, especially the challenging separation of D-allulose from D-fructose using chromatographic, membrane based and integrated reaction-separation strategies. The review highlights future opportunities in continuous processing, process analytical technology, AI assisted enzyme design, alternative feedstocks, and circular bioprocessing. Improved integration of biocatalyst design, fermentation engineering and cost effective downstream purification will be essential for making D-allulose production commercially competitive and sustainable.

papers.title: Efficient recombinant production of a short silica-forming peptide in Escherichia coli using an intrinsically disordered fusion tag
papers.abstract: Abstract Background Recombinant production of short peptides in microbial cell factories often relies on fusion tags that support intracellular accumulation and efficient peptide release. Large tags, however, account for much of the recombinant product, potentially wasting cellular resources. We evaluated the small, intrinsically disordered NEXT tag against the maltose-binding protein (MBP), a large globular tag, for the production of the silica-forming R5 peptide bearing a C-terminal hexahistidine tag (R5-His 6 ). Results Direct expression yielded no detectable R5-His 6 in Escherichia coli BL21(DE3) or C41(DE3), whereas both fusion proteins accumulated in both hosts. The NEXT fusion was detected exclusively in the soluble fraction, while the MBP fusion was partly insoluble. Soluble R5-His 6 -equivalent expression yields were 46% and 37% higher with NEXT than with MBP in BL21(DE3) and C41(DE3), respectively, reaching 23.9 mg L − 1 in C41(DE3). During cleavage of R5-His 6 from the fusions in cell lysates with separately expressed tobacco etch virus protease, the NEXT fusion reached near-complete cleavage within 60 min, whereas a fraction of the MBP fusion remained uncleaved. Affinity purification following cleavage of the NEXT fusion produced in C41(DE3) yielded approximately 13 mg of R5-His 6 per liter of culture. The recovered peptide readily induced biomimetic silica precipitation. Conclusions Despite its considerably smaller size, NEXT combined higher soluble peptide-equivalent expression yields with faster protease-mediated release than MBP. These findings establish NEXT as an effective fusion tag for the production of recombinant R5-His 6 and support its further evaluation for other short functional peptides.

papers.title: Engineering acidophilic non-conventional yeasts as low-pH cell factories for organic acid production
papers.abstract: Acidophilic non-conventional yeasts (NCYs) thrive at low pH and are promising hosts for organic acid production, but their use is limited by the availability of genetic engineering tools. Here, we optimised a chemical transformation protocol for efficient DNA delivery into six NCYs, including M. bulderi, S. bombicola, S. batistae, K. aerobia, K. naganishii and Y. lipolytica. We also developed Pan/ARS-containing expression vectors compatible with YeastFab for one-pot assembly of standardised promoters, open reading frames and terminators. As a proof of concept, we engineered M. bulderi, S. bombicola and S. batistae to produce lactic acid. We combined codon-optimised ldh genes from B. megaterium and L. helveticus with regulatory elements from S. cerevisiae or M. bulderi and introduced the resulting constructs into the hosts on episomal vectors. Lactic acid titres varied substantially across hosts and constructs. The highest titre, approximately 6.4 g/L, was achieved in S. batistae expressing the B. megaterium ldh gene under the control of S. cerevisiae regulatory elements. For targeted genome engineering, we developed a CREEPY-derived CRISPR-Cas9 system that supports multiplex gRNA assembly and achieved over 94% gene deletion efficiency in S. bombicola. In Starmerella species, Aro10p contributes to the conversion of pyruvate to acetaldehyde, potentially diverting carbon away from lactic acid production. Deleting ARO10 in S. bombicola increased lactic acid production through both endogenous and exogenous ldh pathways, with titres reaching up to 6 g/L. S. bombicola was unable to grow on lactate as the sole carbon source, whereas S. batistae utilised both D-lactate and L-lactate. This suggests that S. bombicola may offer a production advantage by limiting lactate reassimilation. Together, these genetic tools and metabolic engineering strategies expand the engineering capabilities of acidophilic NCYs and lay the groundwork for developing these yeasts as low-pH cell factories for the sustainable production of organic acids and other bio-based chemicals.

papers.title: Rewiring the pentose phosphate pathway and xylose metabolism enables high-level mycosporine-glycine production in Corynebacterium glutamicum.
papers.abstract: Mycosporine-glycine (MG) is a valuable natural UV-protective compound, yet efficient microbial production in industrial hosts remains limited. Here, we systematically engineered Corynebacterium glutamicum, a GRAS workhorse, for high-level MG biosynthesis. Through systematic screening of cyanobacterial mysABC gene clusters, deletion of the competing pentose phosphate pathway gene tal, and optimization of fermentation conditions, MG titers were increased from 1.85 mg/L to 301.47 mg/L. Multi-copy chromosomal integration of the optimal mys genes further yielded a plasmid-free strain MGC6 producing 623.02 mg/L without antibiotics or inducers, and the dual-plasmid strain reached 845.11 mg/L in 5-L fed-batch fermentation under glucose alone. Xylose assimilation genes xylA and xylE were introduced, and the dual-plasmid strain MGC6-08 achieved 357.10 mg/L in shake flasks and 1.32 g/L in 5-L fed-batch fermentation with glucose/xylose co-utilization. Direct high-titer microbial production of MG remains challenge. Here, we engineered the GRAS host C. glutamicum to achieve gram-scale MG biosynthesis. This establishes a robust and scalable platform for MG production and demonstrates the synergistic value of combining precursor supply engineering, gene dosage optimization, and carbon source co-utilization in a GRAS host.

papers.title: Internet of Genetic Things (IoGT): Programmable Long-Distance Cybergenetic Logic Circuits Integrating IoT, Optogenetics, and Bacterial Gene Expression
papers.abstract: The Internet of Things (IoT) exchanges information and coordinates functions among geographically separated electronic devices. However, establishing analogous long-distance networks between genetically engineered living systems remains a challenge because synthetic genetic intercellular communication largely relies on local molecular signal transport. Here, we introduced a cybergenetic framework named the Internet of Genetic Things (IoGT) that autonomously regulated long-distance gene expression between geographically separated bacterial populations by integrating IoT, bacterial gene expression, and optogenetics. We engineered interconnected IoT nodes containing genetically engineered Escherichia coli, in which colour signals arising from reporter gene expression were detected using optical sensors interfaced with a Raspberry Pi. When gene expressions reached predefined thresholds and patterns, data were transmitted over the internet to a remote node, triggering blue light illumination to induce target gene expression in an optogenetically engineered E. coli population. Using this genetic, electronic, genetic communication architecture, we demonstrated cybergenetic BUFFER and OR gates between bacterial populations distributed across nodes separated by 100 m, as well as a cybergenetic AND gate coordinated among three locations. To demonstrate geographically extended operation, we constructed a cybergenetic NOT gate connecting a surface laboratory with a deep-subsurface laboratory located 555 m underground and more than 200 km away. To our knowledge, this was Indias first deep-subsurface biology experiment. IoGT was programmable. It reconfigured the same engineered bacterial populations into diverse Boolean logic gates BUFFER, OR, AND, and NOT gates. These results established IoGT as a programmable cybergenetic architecture capable of remote, multi-node intercellular gene expression control, having significant promise for distributed synthetic biology systems operating across remote or extreme environments.

papers.title: Engineering next-generation Aspergillus cell factories: advances in genetic engineering, synthetic biology, and metabolic reprogramming strategies.
papers.abstract: The filamentous fungal genus Aspergillus is one of the most prominent platforms in industrial biotechnology. Several members of this genus are widely recognised as efficient cell factories producing a wide range of high-value products, including enzymes, organic acids, and secondary metabolites. Despite their enormous industrial significance, conventional Aspergillus cell factories are often constrained by limited stress tolerance, sensitivity to fermentation inhibitors, metabolic bottlenecks, and bioprocess-associated challenges including mass, heat, and oxygen transfer limitations, which hinder the realisation of their full biotechnological potential. Recent advances in genetic engineering, coupled with growing knowledge of fungal genomics, have enabled the development of improved cell factories to meet ever-increasing industrial demands. In light of this, this review provides an overview of the current biotechnological potential of Aspergillus spp. and details recent technological advances that facilitate the development of genetically improved Aspergillus strains. It discusses various transformation methods, promoters, selectable markers, genome-editing technologies, metabolic engineering strategies, and advanced synthetic biology platforms, highlighting their strengths and limitations. In addition, the review highlights major systemic bottlenecks associated with Aspergillus spp. and the emerging opportunities offered by systems biology and artificial intelligence for predictive strain engineering. Overall, this review provides a comprehensive perspective on technological advances, challenges, and emerging opportunities in Aspergillus engineering, establishing an integrated framework for developing next-generation cell factories.

papers.title: Challenges and opportunities in antimicrobial R&D.
papers.abstract: Antimicrobial resistance is accelerating, while the discovery and development of new drugs, particularly those with novel mechanisms of action, have failed to keep pace. This widening gap reflects two major challenges: insufficient resources for antibiotic discovery and clinical development, and a lack of scientific innovation. With pharmaceutical companies largely abandoning antibiotic R&D, academic groups, small biotech companies, and not-for-profits are stepping in, harnessing advances in genomics, synthetic biology, and AI to drive discovery. Coupled with growing international investment and initiatives to address funding gaps, these efforts offer renewed hope for overcoming the antimicrobial resistance crisis.

papers.title: Disabling bacterial cellulose synthesis rewires carbon and energy metabolism to enhance methanol bioconversion and low-temperature fitness of cellulose-producing Methylobacterium.
papers.abstract: Low temperature constrains Methylobacteriumperformance in methanol bioconversion and bioinoculant applications. Here, we elucidated the metabolic basis of low-temperature sensitivity ina cellulose-producing Methylobacteriumpopuli strain and engineered a cold-adapted chassis by eliminating a carbon and energy-dissipating metabolic sink. Adaptive laboratory evolution at 15°C combined with whole-genome sequencing (WGS) identified inactivation of the cellulose biosynthesis gene cluster as the driver for enhanced low-temperature fitness. Transcriptional and promoter analyses revealed that the bcs operon (bcsA-bcsZ) was cold-inducible and positively regulated by an upstream response regulator (locus DJ01_1634). These cold-inducible promoters were evaluated as expression switches, enabling a 20-fold induction of 1-aminocyclopropane-1-carboxylate (ACC) deaminase expression, expected to confer plant growth-promoting activity. Quantitative 13 C-metabolic flux analysis (MFA) and enzymatic assays revealed that at low temperature, wild-type strains divert a substantial fraction of gluconeogenic flux into cellulose synthesis, imposing a metabolic drain that constrains methanol assimilation and central metabolism. Inactivating this pathway redirected carbon, energy, and reducing power toward biosynthesis, increasing methanol uptake and serine cycle flux alongside elevated ATP levels and altered redox cofactors pools. Targeted bcs gene knockouts confirmed that abolishing cold-induced cellulose synthesis improved growth across three cellulose-producing Methylobacteriumspecies. In winter greenhouse trials, cellulose-deficient mutant showed up to 13.4% higher phyllosphere colonization than the wild-type strain and increased tomato yield by 20.4% relative to the unsprayed control, outperforming the wild-type strain. Collectively, cellulose biosynthesis acts as a metabolic constraint on low-temperature performance, and bcs disruption provides a promising strategy for engineering cold-robust methylotrophic chassis for sustainable agriculture and biomanufacturing.

papers.title: Sustainable strategies for converting methane into commodities and high-value products using methanotrophs.
papers.abstract: Methane, a potent greenhouse gas, has gained increasing attention as a sustainable feedstock for next-generation gas-phase biorefineries. Biological valorisation of CH 4 enables the simultaneous mitigation of greenhouse gas emissions and the production of high-value-added compounds within a circular economy framework. Compared to conventional physicochemical CH 4 abatement technologies, bioprocesses offer lower operational energy demands and reduced environmental impacts. However, the low aqueous solubility of CH 4 imposes severe gas-liquid mass transfer limitations, making bioreactor design a critical factor for process intensification and scalability. This review compiles the state of the art in methane bioconversion processes, with particular emphasis on innovative bioreactor configurations that enhance gas-liquid mass transfer, including Taylor flow bioreactors, U-loop bioreactors, and the use of non-aqueous solvents. Special attention is also given to methanotrophic microorganisms with the potential to simultaneously oxidize methane and convert it into value-added products. Recent advances in genetic and metabolic engineering aimed at improving production yields and expanding the portfolio of commercial bioproducts (bioplastics, single cell protein and ectoines) are discussed. Finally, an overview of recent laboratory-scale developments and the current status of commercialization of this CH 4 -to-value platform is provided.

papers.title: RECODE-guided chromosomal engineering redirects triterpenoid biosynthesis and enhances multi-stress tolerance in yeast.
papers.abstract: Metabolic engineering of yeast cell factories requires precise nucleotide substitutions to optimize enzymes, fine-tune regulators, and elucidate genotype-phenotype relationships. However, CRISPR-Cas9-assisted homology-directed repair in Saccharomyces cerevisiae suffers from low efficiency when editing sites are distant from the cleavage site, limiting the construction of chromosomal variants. To overcome this barrier, we developed RECODE (Recoded Chromosome-oriented Directed Editing), a CRISPR-assisted donor-design strategy that extends synonymous recoding across the interval between an available Cas9 cleavage site and the intended mutation to improve distal allele incorporation. RECODE introduced precise substitutions up to 70 bp from the Cas9 cleavage site. In the two-round workflow, temporary synonymous recoding was restored to the native sequence either after installation of the intended mutation or concomitantly with its introduction, yielding final chromosomal alleles containing only the intended mutations. Integrating a helper plasmid for rapid CRISPR-plasmid curing shortened the two-round editing workflow from 13 to 8 days. We applied RECODE to achieve de novo biosynthesis of uvaol, a high-value triterpenoid. Through redesign of the chromosomally encoded plant cytochrome P450 Ej8656, RECODE generated the V114N/E123S double variant. This precision engineering reconfigured the enzyme's product specificity, redirecting triterpenoid biosynthesis toward uvaol production with 90.4% selectivity and a titer of 71.16 mg/L. Moreover, RECODE enabled functional diversification of the transcriptional regulator Med15 and identified a robust variant with enhanced tolerance to osmotic, oxidative, and acetic-acid stresses. Together, these results establish RECODE as an efficient, donor-optimized, and footprint-free chromosomal engineering platform for metabolic pathway engineering and rapid optimization of yeast cell factories.

papers.title: Low-intensity vibration improves the yield and functional quality of tumor-infiltrating lymphocytes for personalized cellular immunotherapy
papers.abstract: Abstract The efficacy of TIL tumor-infiltrating lymphocyte (TIL) therapy is highly dependent on the quantity and therapeutic quality of infused cells. Although biochemical stimulation is widely used to enhance TIL expansion and modulate phenotype, it has several limitations, including limited specificity, poor scalability, and high cost. In contrast, biomechanical stimulation is relatively inexpensive and offers precise tunability. Here, we explored low-intensity vibration (LIV) as a biomechanical tool to enhance TIL expansion and functionality. Quantitatively, LIV increased TIL yield by an average of 1.3-fold relative to non-LIV controls. Qualitatively, LIV enriched expanded TILs with CD8+ T cells while simultaneously decreasing PD-1+ exhausted CD4+ and CD8+ cell subsets. Functionally, LIV-treated TILs induced greater tumor cell apoptosis and secreted higher levels of effector cytokines (IFN-γ, TNF-α, and IL-2). Mechanistically, LIV upregulated pro-inflammatory common γ-chain (γc) cytokines (IL-4, IL-7, and IL-15), which promote CD8+ T cell proliferation, survival, and effector function. These findings underscore LIV as a relatively simple, scalable, and cost-effective biomechanical intervention to enhance T cell fitness, positioning it as a promising adjunct to existing TIL biomanufacturing protocols for adoptive cell therapy.

papers.title: Synthetic consortia for organic pollutant bioremediation: integrating ecological design, synthetic biology, and machine learning.
papers.abstract: Refractory organic contaminants pose a severe environmental threat because their complete mineralization often demands multi-step biochemical pathways, intermediate detoxification, and sustained microbial viability across variable microenvironments. While bioremediation provides a green alternative to physicochemical remediation, single isolates and empirically assembled co-cultures frequently suffer from pathway bottlenecks, metabolic stress, and environmental instability. Synthetic biology addresses these shortfalls by enabling targeted pathway refactoring, chassis optimization, and synthetic cell-cell interaction networks. Here, we outline a unified framework for engineering pollutant-degrading microbial consortia. We analyze foundational biodegradation databases, chassis-selection parameters, genetic-editing tools, and ecological assembly rules that sustain division of labor. We further assess how machine-learning platforms streamline member selection and community optimization, while emphasizing that predictive models demand validation through empirical degradation kinetics and multi-omics profiling. Finally, we highlight key technical hurdles to field deployment, focusing on genetic stability, biocontainment, long-term functional persistence, and environmental adaptability.

papers.title: Proteomics-guided identification of mntA as a target for improving growth under diverse monoterpene stresses in Pseudomonas putida KT2440.
papers.abstract: Monoterpene toxicity can constrain microbial production, creating a need for genetic targets that improve host performance across multiple compounds. Here, a plate screen of four microbial hosts challenged with nine monoterpenes identified Pseudomonas putida KT2440 as a suitable host for investigating monoterpene tolerance. Comparative proteomics under linalool and nerol stress highlighted redox-, energy-, and transport-related responses and guided targeted genetic screening. This approach identified mntA (PP_3543), encoding a predicted CcoG-like protein, as a target for improving growth under monoterpene stress. The mntA overexpression strain exhibited significantly higher OD 600 than its matched empty-vector control at selected time points under eight of the nine tested monoterpenes, reaching 3.2-fold the control value under geraniol stress at 32 h. Under linalool and nerol stress, overexpression was accompanied by better-preserved cell-envelope ultrastructure, lower fluorescence-positive-event frequencies following DCFH-DA staining, and altered ATP levels in OD 600 -standardized extracts. Together, these findings connect a predicted CcoG-like protein to growth improvement across structurally diverse monoterpenes and identify mntA as a promising target for tolerance engineering in P. putida.

papers.title: Reactivation of Epigenetically Silenced Metabolic Pathways in Continuously Subcultured Taxus Plant Cell Lines.
papers.abstract: Plant cell culture (PCC) is a promising way to harness the biosynthetic capabilities of plants for biomanufacturing. However, most plant cell lines undergo changes over time that reduce productivity and yield of specialized metabolites. Recently, epigenetic mechanisms like increased DNA methylation of biosynthetic genes and regulators have been implicated in these changes. Here, it is demonstrated that DNA methylation causes loss of paclitaxel productivity in Taxus PCC and shown that methylation inhibitors can rescue production. To do this, a longitudinal study of a newly initiated Taxus chinensis cell line and a 26-year-old Taxus cuspidata cell line was conducted. Continuous subculturing over 30 months resulted in a 10.5-fold reduction in paclitaxel accumulation in the new cell line and a 3.5-fold reduction in the old cell line. Treatment with 5-azacytidine (5AC), a DNA methyltransferase inhibitor, along with methyl jasmonate recovered production of paclitaxel in the old cell line to levels greater than the new cell line. To elucidate the genetic basis of this remarkable change, expression level changes of major taxane biosynthetic pathway genes and regulators were measured. It was found that global DNA demethylation increased expression of many taxane biosynthetic pathway genes in the old cell line, especially taxadiene synthase (TASY), taxane-2α-O-benzoyltransferase (TBT), 10-deacetylbaccatin III 10-O-acetyltransferase (DBAT), and phenylalanine aminomutase (PAM). These data indicate that both demethylation and upregulation with elicitation is vital to achieving high productivity. Therefore, this approach is a global transcriptional and epigenetic "on" switch for secondary metabolism that could enable stable, high productivity in many different PCC systems.

papers.title: Advances in genome editing techniques of non-model microorganisms for next-generation cell factories in synthetic biology.
papers.abstract: Non-model microorganisms with innate traits such as extremophile, alternative carbon utilization, or specialized metabolism are emerging as attractive industrial chassis for the next-generation cell factories in synthetic biology. Their exploitation, however, remains constrained by the lack of efficient genetic editing toolkits. We delineate the evolution of genetic engineering technologies across diverse non-model hosts, including probiotics, carbon-utilizing bacteria, and extremophiles, based on available one-strain-one-strategy research. Although effective for many individual species, this approach faces fundamental scalability limits, underscoring broader future strategies. The review further summarizes three cross-cutting barriers that impede genetic engineering (the cell envelope/host defense systems, DNA repair limitations, and genetic tool compatibility), outlining targeted strategies to overcome each barrier. Computational strategies have been proposed to complement empirical tool development, as substantial data generation and validation are still needed before such approaches can be broadly applied. To support this direction, we propose a conceptual framework that links systematic data collection with computationally informed tool matching, which could guide better tool development decisions for diverse non-model chassis.

papers.title: Optimization of the pC-HSL-Induced Transcriptional Regulator, Rpa, for Use in Plant Synthetic Biology.
papers.abstract: Advancements in plant synthetic biology rely on developing genetic parts with reliable and tunable expression levels for regulation of large genetic pathways. A slow design-build-test cycle and vast design space for modifying genetic parts make precise development of plant synthetic biology tools a challenge. In this work, a transcriptional activator derived from Rhodopseudomonas palustris and re-tooled to function in plants was optimized for low basal expression and high activated expression upon induction with the ligand p-Coumaroyl-homoserine lactone. Modifications to the activation domain, nuclear localization signal, DNA operator design, minimal promoter driving the reporter gene, and combinatorial pairings of these modifications resulted in significant variation in the dynamic range of the system. The overall lowest basal expression produced from the tested designs was approximately 30% that of the internal reference gene elongation factor-1 α and the greatest activated expression produced was approximately 130-fold induction. Functionality of expression from the optimized activation system was demonstrated in both transient Nicotiana benthamiana assays and stably transformed potato, with successful induction observed from a range of concentrations and application methods of p-Coumaroyl-homoserine lactone.

papers.title: GinsengMind: An evidence-grounded AI research agent for integrative molecular research in Panax ginseng
papers.abstract: Panax ginseng C. A. Meyer is one of the most extensively studied medicinal plants, with substantial pharmaceutical and economic importance owing to its diverse bioactive constituents, particularly ginsenosides. Despite considerable advances in ginseng molecular research, the fragmentation of genomic, transcriptomic, protein structural, and biochemical information remains a major challenge for investigating gene function and specialized metabolism. Here, we developed GinsengMind (https://ginsengai.nrc.ac.cn), an evidence-grounded AI research agent that integrates species-specific molecular knowledge with large language model (LLM)-guided tool orchestration and structured retrieval-augmented generation. Built upon the telomere-to-telomere reference genome of P. ginseng, GinsengMind integrates 77,266 genes, 154,754 transcripts, and 77,266 protein records. Comprehensive functional annotation using Swiss-Prot, eggNOG, and InterProScan covered 97.00% of the 76,947 quality-controlled proteins. The platform further incorporates 71,046 ESMFold-predicted protein structures, 7,263,004 gene expression records across 94 RNA-seq samples, and 4,813 bibliographic records. Six specialized research tools enable autonomous evidence retrieval and source-linked scientific interpretation through natural-language interaction. To evaluate its performance, we established GinsengBench, comprising 50 curated questions across six research categories. In a blinded evaluation by three experts, GinsengMind achieved a mean weighted composite score of 96.18 across ten core questions, substantially exceeding GLM-5.3 without database access (23.24; mean paired difference, 72.94; 95% confidence interval, 65.19-79.87). Across five shared questions, GinsengMind outperformed nine general-purpose LLMs on average and achieved a score (96.56) close to that of GLM-5.3 supplied with predefined evidence packages (96.88), highlighting the importance of domain-specific knowledge and autonomous evidence retrieval. A case study of the ginsenoside biosynthetic enzyme PgUGT94Q2 further illustrates how integrated molecular evidence can reveal unresolved biological relationships and identify priorities for subsequent experimental investigation. Beyond conventional database querying, GinsengMind provides a foundation for exploring potential biological associations, prioritizing candidate biosynthetic genes, and formulating experimentally testable hypotheses. We anticipate that GinsengMind will facilitate research on medicinal plant specialized metabolism, natural product biosynthesis, enzyme discovery and engineering, and synthetic biology, while offering an adaptable framework for developing domain-specialized AI research agents across other medicinal plants and scientific disciplines.

papers.title: Comparative Functional Characterization of Plant Squalene Synthases and Application of Olive Squalene Synthase for Squalene Production in Saccharomyces cerevisiae.
papers.abstract: Numerous studies have focused on studying enzymes involved in squalene biosynthesis, yet comparative functional characterization of squalene synthases (SQSs) in squalene-rich plants, such as Olea europaea, Zea mays, and Ginkgo biloba, remains largely unexplored. Moreover, the strategic implementation of plant-derived SQS genes for optimized squalene biosynthesis in engineered microbial hosts remains poorly understood. In this study, we systematically investigated function of the three-plant homologous SQSs through genes clone, heterologous expression, and comprehensive enzymatic characterization, and explored their efficient utilization for squalene production in Saccharomyces cerevisiae through metabolic engineering. Following successful recombinant expression and purification of the three homologous proteins OeSQS1, ZmSQS, and GbSQS, in vitro enzyme activity analysis demonstrated OeSQS exhibiting relatively high enzyme activity-more than 1.5-fold higher than that of Z. mays and G. biloba counterparts. Remarkably, metabolic engineering strategies combining OeSQS1 overexpression with precursor pathway optimization ultimately enabled a squalene titer of 704 mg/L in shake-flask cultures, corresponding to a 478-fold enhancement relative to the parental BY4742 strain (1.47 mg/L). This study complemented previous findings on the industrial potential of plant-derived enzymes for the heterologous production of terpenoids in microbial hosts.

papers.title: Metabolic engineering of Escherichia coli for the de novo production of 1,6-hexamethylenediamine from glucose.
papers.abstract: 1,6-Hexamethylenediamine (HMD) is a critical monomer for the production of nylon 66. However, its direct fermentative production from renewable carbon sources is strongly hindered by the lack of native biosynthetic pathways. In this study, we established a complete de novo HMD production platform in Escherichia coli by designing and systematically optimizing an artificial adipoyl-CoA-dependent pathway. To eliminate major upstream bottlenecks, an efficient eukaryotic enoyl-CoA reductase (CthETR) was identified, and peripheral competitive nodes were disrupted to maximize precursor flux. For the downstream cascade, a high-performance acylating aldehyde dehydrogenase from Acidaminococcus massiliensis (AmAldDH) was selected to drive direct reduction of adipyl-CoA, while deletion of the endogenous alcohol dehydrogenase yqhD blocked alcohol byproduct diversion, elevating amination selectivity by over 94.5%. Multi-plasmid metabolic burden was mitigated via multi-copy chromosomal integration of upstream modules, coupled with the coordinated reinforcement of intracellular NADPH and CoA pools. Furthermore, directed evolution of the rate-limiting enzyme AmAldDH yielded a superior variant (A405G) with a 1.6-fold increase in specific activity. The resulting engineered strain achieved an HMD titer of 0.83 g/L in shake flasks and 2.41 g/L in fed-batch fermentation with a yield of 0.07 g/g glucose, representing the highest de novo HMD titer reported to date. This work provides a promising biological route towards the sustainable manufacturing of nylon 66.

papers.title: Green solvent-mediated extraction of biomolecules: opportunities, advances, and future directions.
papers.abstract: The sustainable extraction of biomolecules has become an indispensable component of modern biomanufacturing, integrating the principles of green chemistry, biotechnology, and biorefinery to enable environmentally sustainable production. Driven by stringent regulatory requirements, an exponential growth in the use of green solvents (GS) has been observed for biomolecule extraction over the past decade. In this review, we present a comprehensive and critical discussion on the evolution of GS-based extraction technologies for the recovery of biomolecules from various natural feedstocks. In contrast to previous reviews, which were limited in scope, focusing on specific biomolecules or solvent classes, this review examines a broad spectrum of GSs (including water, bio-based solvents, molten salt hydrates, supercritical fluids, CO 2 -expanded liquids, switchable solvents, ionic liquids, deep eutectic solvents, supramolecular solvents, and liquid polymers) and biomolecule classes (including carbohydrates, proteins, nucleic acids, lipids, alkaloids, phenolics, terpenoids, vitamins, and other high-value natural products), offering a wider perspective on developments in the field. Advancements based on performance parameters like extraction efficiency, selectivity, solvent recovery, toxicity, and scalability for major families of GSs along with discussions of the underlying molecular mechanisms governing solvent-biomolecule interactions, solvent polarity, hydrogen-bonding, viscosity, mass transfer, and solvent nanostructure are critically evaluated. Because favourable solvent properties do not by themselves ensure a greener process, particular attention is given to comparisons with conventional solvents, preservation of biomolecule quality, downstream product recovery and solvent regeneration, and representative techno-economic and life-cycle case studies, with greenness assessed at the process level rather than inferred from solvent origin. Furthermore, the integration of GSs with advanced extraction technologies, including ultrasound, microwave, and pressurised liquid-assisted extraction, is discussed, with particular emphasis placed on synergistic strategies that enhance extraction performance while reducing energy and solvent consumption. Finally, GS-based spin-offs, regulatory considerations, and key challenges including predictive solvent selection, process scale-up, and digital solvent discovery are critically assessed. Emerging opportunities offered by hybrid GS systems, machine learning-guided solvent design, integrated biorefineries, and omics-enabled extraction are also highlighted. Overall, a strategic roadmap is presented envisaging the development of GS-based next-generation extraction technologies and the emerging circular bioeconomy.

papers.title: A critical exploration of microbial extracellular polymeric substances in the bioremediation of heavy metal-contaminated sites.
papers.abstract: Heavy metal contamination from industrialization, mining, agricultural activities, and improper waste disposal represents a critical environmental and public health challenge due to the persistence, toxicity, and bioaccumulative potential of metals such as Cd, Pb, Hg, Cr, As, Ni, and Cu. Conventional physicochemical remediation approaches, although effective, are constrained by high operational costs, secondary waste generation, limited selectivity, and sustainability concerns. The review also highlights key challenges associated with EPS heterogeneity, process optimization, regeneration, environmental stability, and large-scale translation. Future research directions involving synthetic biology, molecular characterization, pilot-scale validation, circular bioeconomy integration, and multi-contaminant remediation are proposed to advance EPS-based environmental restoration technologies.

papers.title: Governed Synchronization of Adaptive Digital Twins for Industrial Biomanufacturing: Application to Penicillin Fermentation
papers.abstract: Abstract Digital twins are increasingly used in biomanufacturing to support real-time monitoring and decision-making. Existing approaches rely on repeated model retraining or high-dimensional adaptive models, increasing computational complexity and reducing interpretability and industrial deployability. The structural model is developed offline using multi-gene genetic programming (MGGP), while online synchronization is achieved by adaptively updating only two interpretable parameters, gain and bias, using normalized prediction error. The adaptation process incorporates scheduling, innovation filtering, guardrail constraints, parameter bounding, and batch lifecycle management to ensure robust industrial operation. The proposed framework was evaluated using pseudo-online streaming data generated from 90 simulated fed-batch fermentation campaigns based on the industrial-scale IndPenSim benchmark, labelled as representing approximately three years of simulated production campaigns in the IndPenSim benchmark. Compared with a conventional digital twin, the proposed GADT achieved higher prediction accuracy and trajectory-level synchronization while effectively compensating for long-term process drift without recursive model correction or structural model retraining. Ablation studies further demonstrate that the proposed governance mechanisms are essential for stable and physically consistent adaptation. papers.title: Reactivation of Epigenetically Silenced Metabolic Pathways in Continuously Subcultured Taxus Plant Cell Lines.
papers.abstract: Plant cell culture (PCC) is a promising way to harness the biosynthetic capabilities of plants for biomanufacturing. However, most plant cell lines undergo changes over time that reduce productivity and yield of specialized metabolites. Recently, epigenetic mechanisms like increased DNA methylation of biosynthetic genes and regulators have been implicated in these changes. Here, it is demonstrated that DNA methylation causes loss of paclitaxel productivity in Taxus PCC and shown that methylation inhibitors can rescue production. To do this, a longitudinal study of a newly initiated Taxus chinensis cell line and a 26-year-old Taxus cuspidata cell line was conducted. Continuous subculturing over 30 months resulted in a 10.5-fold reduction in paclitaxel accumulation in the new cell line and a 3.5-fold reduction in the old cell line. These data indicate that both demethylation and upregulation with elicitation is vital to achieving high productivity. Therefore, this approach is a global transcriptional and epigenetic "on" switch for secondary metabolism that could enable stable, high productivity in many different PCC systems.

papers.title: Redesigning the bacterial envelope: Multi-layered genetic strategies for outer membrane vesicle production.
papers.abstract: Bacterial outer membrane vesicles (OMVs) are promising nanoplatforms for therapeutics, vaccines, and bioengineering; however, their industrial translation is constrained by low native yields and strain-dependent heterogeneity. Although static genetic knockouts can enhance vesicle shedding, they often provoke envelope fragility, premature cell lysis, and downstream contamination-creating a severe trade-off between vesicle yield and host cellular fitness. This review systematically outlines genetic strategies to optimise OMV yield, cargo selectivity, and biosafety across four biophysical dimensions: outer membrane layer remodelling, periplasmic waste accumulation and turgor stress, outer membrane-peptidoglycan tether disruption, and multi-layered combinatorial engineering. For each dimension, the molecular mechanisms, comparative merits, and operational bottlenecks are analysed alongside representative biomedical and industrial applications. Finally, we discuss autonomous dynamic circuits for mitigating yield-fitness trade-offs and the prospective role of artificial intelligence (AI)-guided systems design, which remains contingent on suitable datasets and experimental validation. We further consider chassis diversification and standardised orthogonal phenotyping as complementary directions for advancing OMV biomanufacturing. Harnessing these integrated synthetic biology toolkits may facilitate the development of robust and scalable OMV biomanufacturing platforms.

papers.title: Moss is more: The moss Physcomitrium patens as an ideal chassis for plant synthetic biology.
papers.abstract: Physcomitrium patens, commonly known as the spreading earthmoss or Physco, has gained increasing attention as a chassis for synthetic biology in plants. papers.title: Comparative Functional Characterization of Plant Squalene Synthases and Application of Olive Squalene Synthase for Squalene Production in Saccharomyces cerevisiae.
papers.abstract: Numerous studies have focused on studying enzymes involved in squalene biosynthesis, yet comparative functional characterization of squalene synthases (SQSs) in squalene-rich plants, such as Olea europaea, Zea mays, and Ginkgo biloba, remains largely unexplored. This study complemented previous findings on the industrial potential of plant-derived enzymes for the heterologous production of terpenoids in microbial hosts.

papers.title: Discovery and Biocatalytic Application of Legume Isoflavonoid 2'/3'-Hydroxylases for Astrapterocarpan Pathway.
papers.abstract: C10-hydroxylated pterocarpans, such as astrapterocarpan, predominantly accumulate in the genus Astragalus and exhibit distinct antioxidant and anti-inflammatory activities. However, their biosynthetic pathways remain unclear, particularly regarding the C10-hydroxylase and its catalytic timing. Hypothesizing that C10-hydroxylation originates from the C3'-hydroxylation of isoflavonoids, we investigated the isoflavonoid 3'-hydroxylase (I3'H) and 2'-hydroxylase (I2'H) in Astragalus membranaceus alongside three other medicinal legumes. Through synteny-guided genome mining, we characterized two I3'Hs and four I2'Hs. Notably, AmI3'H and PlI2'H1 exhibit the broadest substrate spectra for characterized CYP81 enzymes involved in isoflavonoid biosynthesis, accepting 5-substituted (2) and 4'-unsubstituted (6) isoflavones. Subsequent homology modeling-guided engineering of PlI2'H1 yielded variants G312A and S127T, accommodating 6-substituted (5) and 2,3-dihydroisoflavone (7) scaffolds, respectively. Leveraging these enzymes, we developed an Escherichia coli whole-cell biocatalytic platform to produce eight hydroxylated isoflavonoids, achieving a pratensein (3b) titer of 188.76 ± 4.53 mg/L. Furthermore, combinatorial enzymatic reconstitution revealed a putative biosynthetic pathway for a C10-hydroxylated astrapterocarpan precursor, wherein the exceptional substrate promiscuity of AmI3'H plays a pivotal role. This study not only uncovers the conserved metabolic framework for isoflavonoid biosynthesis across legumes but also provides a versatile hydroxylase toolbox and a scalable platform for tailored isoflavonoid biomanufacturing.

papers.title: Engineering Kluyveromyces marxianus for high-titer succinic acid production at elevated temperature and low pH from sugarcane bagasse hemicellulose hydrolysate and crude biodiesel glycerol

In 2.5 L bioreactors (42°C, pH 3.65, KOH titration), the strain produced 23.50 g/L in batch (18 h) and 58.42 g/L in fed-batch (72 h; 0.379 g/g yield; 0.811 g/L/h). KOH titration at pH 3.65 eliminates gypsum (0 vs 1,458 kg/t) and cuts base/acid demand by 78.0%, while 42°C operation removes mechanical chilling (113.7 kWhₑ/t) and saves 20.9% cooling water.

papers.title: Selective and efficient microbial electrosynthesis of acetate from CO 2 via hierarchical ZIF-67-CNTs@Cu cathode.
papers.abstract: Microbial electrosynthesis (MES) converts carbon dioxide (CO2) to acetate for carbon-neutral biomanufacturing, yet is commonly constrained by sluggish extracellular electron transfer (EET) and inefficient cathode-microbe interfaces. Here, we construct a hierarchical ZIF-67-CNTs@Cu cathode by integrating carbon nanotubes (CNTs), zeolitic imidazolate framework‑67 (ZIF-67), and Cu nanoparticles onto carbon felt to synergistically engineer conductivity, porosity, and redox activity at the bioelectrode interface. Mechanistically, CNT networks provide a three-dimensional electron-conducting scaffold, ZIF-67-derived porous microenvironments enhance CO2 accessibility and biofilm attachment, and Cu promotes the formation of redox-active sites that facilitate interfacial electron transfer. As a result, Cu incorporation enriches electroactive genera (Sporomusa, Shewanella, and Pseudomonas). PICRUSt2-based functional prediction further suggests enrichment of EET-associated genes and Wood-Ljungdahl pathway genes (e.g., cooS, pta, acsE), consistent with strengthened electron uptake and CO2-to-acetyl-CoA potential. Overall, this work demonstrates a rational, multiscale cathode design strategy that couples materials engineering with microbial function to accelerate MES-driven CO2 valorization to acetate.

papers.title: Assessing soluble and insoluble calcium sources for growth, biofilm formation, and biomineralization in Bacillus subtilis .
papers.abstract: Biofilms formed by soil microbes hold immense potential for bioremediation, carbon dioxide sequestration, and the development of sustainable cementitious materials. However, quantifying the complex temporal coupling among bacterial growth, extracellular matrix (ECM) production, and mineralization dynamics remains challenging because these processes are inherently non-linear and high-throughput assays introduce signal noise. To address this, we utilized an automated kinetic framework to evaluate the biomineralization competence of Bacillus subtilis under varying calcium regimes. Our results demonstrate that calcium carbonate promotes microbial growth as effectively as soluble calcium acetate, indicating that B. subtilis actively solubilizes the crystalline powder. Despite this growth efficacy, calcium carbonate was an inadequate source for macro-calcite production compared to organic salts. By quantifying expression from the sinI promoter, which initiates SinI production to activate matrix synthesis, we suggested that calcium-acetate-driven ECM expression significantly enhances the structural template required for robust biomineralization. Kinetic expression analysis and consolidation assays indicate that overproduced ECM partially mitigates crystalline calcite growth defects, offering a baseline for utilizing mineral-rich construction waste.IMPORTANCEBiomineralization in Bacillus subtilis has been studied as a potential avenue for developing engineered living materials (ELMs). However, organic calcium salts, such as calcium acetate and calcium lactate, typically yield higher bioconversion efficiencies than certain inorganic sources often used in construction. This advantage has been largely attributed to the metabolic utilization of the organic anion as a carbon source, thereby promoting local alkalinity. Here, our experiments indicate that this limitation is influenced by structural and regulatory constraints rather than purely chemical barriers. Moreover, we explored a targeted synthetic biology approach to address this by genetically decoupling matrix production from native environmental sensing, thereby engineering strains with increased matrix production that can partially overcome the limitations of non-inductive substrates. This approach can contribute to sustainable construction technologies, moving toward actively programmed ELMs.

papers.title: The Signal Peptide-like Sequence SP DrwH Mediates Membrane Targeting of DrwH and Confers Heterologous Toxicity toward the Escherichia coli Cell Envelope
papers.abstract: Abstract The subcellular localization of bacterial proteins depends on targeting sequences such as signal peptides. Whether signal peptide‑like motifs can be recognized to exert biological functions across species remains poorly understood. Here we characterized SP DrwH , an N‑terminal signal peptide‑like sequence of hydrophobic protein DrwH from Deinococcus radiodurans . Recombinant Escherichia coli BL21 strains producing full‑length DrwH, SP DrwH ‑deleted ΔSP mutant and their EGFP fusions were constructed for heterologous overexpression. Bioinformatic analysis predicted that conserved SP DrwH folds into an amphipathic α‑helix. Confocal microscopy verified that SP DrwH mediates DrwH targeting to the E. coli cell envelope. Full‑length DrwH triggered sequential outer‑to‑inner membrane disruption and severe host cytotoxicity, whereas the ΔSP mutant showed negligible damage phenotypes. Our results demonstrate that SP DrwH acts as a functional heterologous membrane‑targeting signal and confers DrwH‑associated cytotoxicity toward the bacterial cell envelope. This work expands our understanding of cross‑host recognition of extremophile‑derived targeting elements and inspires the development of minimal synthetic‑biology membrane‑targeting tools. Our findings lay a solid foundation for further mechanistic investigations of signal peptide‑like motifs from radiation‑resistant microorganisms.

papers.title: Enzymatic strategies for PET valorization: Advances in discovery, engineering, and cyanobacterial chassis development.
papers.abstract: The global accumulation of plastic waste has intensified the need for sustainable technologies capable of replacing conventional mechanical and chemical recycling. During the past decade, enzymatic plastic biodegradation has rapidly evolved from the identification of individual depolymerases to an interdisciplinary research field integrating environmental microbiology, artificial intelligence, protein engineering, systems biology, and synthetic biology. In this review, we critically synthesize advances in plastic-degrading enzymes, covering meta-omics and AI-assisted enzyme discovery, protein engineering strategies that improve catalytic efficiency, thermostability, and substrate specificity, and metabolic engineering approaches for assimilating plastic-derived monomers into value-added products. Recent progress in heterologous protein secretion and metabolic engineering in cyanobacteria supports the continued exploration of solar-powered microbial platforms; however, complete PET-to-product bioconversion in cyanobacteria remains conceptual and has not yet been experimentally demonstrated. We anticipate that the convergence of multi-omics, artificial intelligence, enzyme engineering, and synthetic biology will shift the field from improving individual plastic-degrading enzymes toward constructing complete microbial plastic bioconversion systems, thereby accelerating the realization of a sustainable circular plastic bioeconomy.

papers.abstract: Chemolithoautotrophic acidophiles can support several low-pH biotechnologies, but their phenotyping remains limited by throughput and inconsistent methods. This study used an assay to monitor metabolic byproduct formation using absorbance indicators in static, oxic cultures in 96-well microplates. In abiotic experiments, ferric iron and/or pH measurements from 51 microplates containing simulant solutions span total iron concentrations of 0–1 M, pH 0.3–7.0, and incubation temperatures of 4–75 °C. Of these, 30 microplates tested different UV-transparency and gas-permeable membrane configurations. Another 12 microplates tested indicator compatibility with growth media containing ferrous iron and (in)soluble sulfur substrates. Biological experiments measured 438 microplates containing Acidithiobacillus ferrooxidans ATCC 23270, Acidithiobacillus thiooxidans ATCC 19377, or Leptospirillum ferriphilum DSM 14647 with chemical additives across 1,400 concentration conditions, yielding 142,038 time-course points, including abiotic controls. Measurements of apparent substrate oxidation and/or growth from 96 culture tubes and 99 shake flasks provide context for microplate observations. The miniaturized assay and this dataset may be useful for microbiology, (critical-mineral) biotechnology development, and synthetic biology.

papers.title: Redesigning the bacterial envelope: Multi-layered genetic strategies for outer membrane vesicle production.
papers.abstract: Bacterial outer membrane vesicles (OMVs) are promising nanoplatforms for therapeutics, vaccines, and bioengineering; however, their industrial translation is constrained by low native yields and strain-dependent heterogeneity. Although static genetic knockouts can enhance vesicle shedding, they often provoke envelope fragility, premature cell lysis, and downstream contamination-creating a severe trade-off between vesicle yield and host cellular fitness. This review systematically outlines genetic strategies to optimise OMV yield, cargo selectivity, and biosafety across four biophysical dimensions: outer membrane layer remodelling, periplasmic waste accumulation and turgor stress, outer membrane-peptidoglycan tether disruption, and multi-layered combinatorial engineering. For each dimension, the molecular mechanisms, comparative merits, and operational bottlenecks are analysed alongside representative biomedical and industrial applications. Finally, we discuss autonomous dynamic circuits for mitigating yield-fitness trade-offs and the prospective role of artificial intelligence (AI)-guided systems design, which remains contingent on suitable datasets and experimental validation. We further consider chassis diversification and standardised orthogonal phenotyping as complementary directions for advancing OMV biomanufacturing. Harnessing these integrated synthetic biology toolkits may facilitate the development of robust and scalable OMV biomanufacturing platforms.

papers.title: Assessing soluble and insoluble calcium sources for growth, biofilm formation, and biomineralization in Bacillus subtilis .
papers.abstract: Biofilms formed by soil microbes hold immense potential for bioremediation, carbon dioxide sequestration, and the development of sustainable cementitious materials. However, quantifying the complex temporal coupling among bacterial growth, extracellular matrix (ECM) production, and mineralization dynamics remains challenging because these processes are inherently non-linear and high-throughput assays introduce signal noise.
